When the complement system is activated, it produces C3a and C5a. These are both anaphylatoxins which can cause inflammation. C3a causes degranulation of mast cells and smooth muscle contraction. C5a causes the same as C3a plus it is a potent chemotaxin which attracts phagocytes to the site of infection. C3 convertase is an enzyme which cleaves C3 into C3a and C3b. C3b is involved in immune complex deposition and opsonisation. C3b binds to antigens on pathogens, making them more likely to be engulfed by phagocytes. Phagocytes have a complement receptor on their surface which binds to the C3b coating the pathogen. This enhances phagocytosis. C3b and C5b combine to form the membrane attack complex which punches holes in the pathogen, leading to cell lysis.

Angiotensin I and II is a key component of the Renin-Angiotensin-System (RAS). Angiotensin I is converted to Angiotensin II by ACE. Angiotensin II is a very potent vasopressor and it also causes aldosterone secretion. Aldosterone causes sodium and water retention in the kidneys. Therefore, ACE inhibitors block the production of Angiotensin II. This causes a reduction in aldosterone secretion and therefore a reduction in sodium and water retention. Amnesia is the loss of the ability to recall past events or retain new information.  Amnesia can be an acquired condition, where it occurs after an initial insult, or it can be a normal part of ageing.  Patients with normal ageing do not develop amnesia, whereas patients with mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia do.  Amnesia is a common symptom of Alzheimer's disease, as well as of other dementias including vascular dementia, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, and mixed dementia. The lateral corticospinal tract is the only motor pathway that originates in the cerebral cortex. It is divided into lateral and ventral parts. The lateral part decussates at the pyramids of the medulla and the ventral part descends to the spinal cord to synapse on alpha and gamma motor neurons. The lateral corticospinal tract controls the voluntary rapid dexterous movement at individual digits or joints. The ventral part of the corticospinal tract is an interneuron pathway that decussates in the ventral horn of the spinal cord and synapses on alpha and gamma motor neurons. The medial motor system consists of the rubrospinal, vestibulospinal and tectospinal tracts. These pathways are involved in non-stereotyped movements of the axial and girdle muscles. The rubrospinal tract originates from the red nucleus of the midbrain and decussates in the tegmentum of the pons. It controls non-stereotyped movements of the upper limb muscles. The vestibulospinal tract originates in the vestibular nuclei of the medullary and projects bilaterally to the spinal cord. It controls postural adjustments and balance. The tectospinal tract originates in the superior colliculus of the midbrain and decussates in the tegmentum of the pons. It controls orienting of the eyes and head in response to visual stimuli.
